metadata.description: Historical boundary polygons for Miami and Dade County racialized urban planning
metadata.source: Built by Labor, Divided by Design research project
metadata.note: Polygons are approximations derived from historical accounts and Paul S. George's scholarship. Refinement recommended using georeferenced Sanborn maps.

properties.name: Colored Town / Overtown (1920 approximate boundary)
properties.significance: Miami's segregated Black district, established by deed restrictions and the FEC tracks as de facto racial boundary. Home to large Bahamian and West Indian population alongside African Americans from the US South.
properties.source: Paul S. George, 'Colored Town: Miami's Black Community, 1896-1930' (Florida Historical Quarterly, 1977)

properties.name: West Grove / Little Bahamas (Coconut Grove)
properties.significance: Oldest continuous Bahamian settlement in Miami-Dade; predates Miami incorporation. Charles Ave and Grand Ave corridor. Includes Mariah Brown House, E.W.F. Stirrup House, Charlotte Jane Memorial Cemetery.
properties.source: Marvin Dunn, 'Black Miami in the Twentieth Century' (1997); UMiami Libraries Coconut Grove collections

properties.name: Lemon City
properties.significance: Mixed Black and white community north of Miami; major pineapple farming area in 1890s-1900s; area now part of Little Haiti/Little River

properties.name: Liberty Square Housing Project
properties.significance: One of the first US public housing projects for African Americans; opened Feb 6, 1937. Predecessor: 'Liberty City' subdivision platted by white developer Floyd W. Davis in mid-1920s. A 4-foot concrete wall along NW 12th Ave separated Black residents from white neighborhoods; remnants still stand.
properties.source: UMiami Overtown Chronology; Segregation by Design

properties.name: Liberty City Racial Wall
properties.significance: 4-foot concrete wall along NW 12th Avenue from NW 62nd to NW 71st Streets, physically separating Black residents in Liberty Square from white neighborhoods. Portions still visible.

properties.name: FEC Railway tracks (de facto racial boundary)
properties.significance: The Florida East Coast Railway tracks, running along what is now NW/NE 1st Avenue, served as the racial dividing line from Miami's founding. White downtown developed east; Colored Town west. This geographic feature was the single most important segregation infrastructure in early Miami.
properties.source: Multiple academic sources including Mohl, Connolly, Dunn
